name: Personalized Learning and Tutoring
blurb: For decades, education researchers have pointed to one on one tutoring as one of the most powerful ways to help a student learn. The problem has always been cost, since no school can afford a tutor for every child.
title: Personalized Learning and Tutoring
answer: For decades, education researchers have pointed to one on one tutoring as one of the most powerful ways to help a student learn. The problem has always been cost, since no school can afford a tutor for every child.

papers.why: The strongest evidence in the library for the book's hints not answers theme and for the claim that tool design, not tool presence, decides whether AI helps or harms. It also shows students cannot judge the harm themselves, which supports configured tools over open access for younger grades.
papers.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
papers.venue: PNAS
papers.caveat: One school, one subject, short term outcomes only, run in Fall 2023 with GPT-4; math has objective answers that writing lacks. The guardrailed tutor prevented harm but did not produce a learning gain.
papers.finding: Randomized field experiment with nearly 1,000 students at one Turkish high school, Fall 2023, math review sessions. Three arms: a plain ChatGPT style GPT-4 chat (GPT Base), a guardrailed GPT-4 tutor (GPT Tutor), and no AI. With access during practice, grades rose 48 percent (Base) and 127 percent (Tutor). On a later exam without AI, the Base group scored 17 percent worse than students who never had AI; the Tutor group's harm was essentially eliminated but showed no gain. Base users mostly asked for and copied solutions (a crutch); Tutor users asked for help and attempted answers. Students did not perceive that copying hurt their learning. Guardrails: the prompt included each problem's solution (to curb hallucination), an instruction not to give away the full solution, and teacher supplied common mistakes with matching hints.

papers.why: The clearest positive counterpart to the PNAS harm study: the same class of model improved learning when paired with tutor style prompts, teacher supervision, and curriculum alignment. The authors credit the whole package, not the chatbot alone, which is the book's central argument about implementation over technology.
papers.title: From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria
papers.venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11125
papers.caveat: License recorded from OpenAlex as CC BY; the PDF text extracted here does not state its license, so this is not verified from the document itself. Six weeks, nine urban Benin City schools with computer labs, after school, volunteers, English only. Effect estimates partly reflect extra instructional time with a teacher present; no teacher only tutoring arm.
papers.finding: Randomized trial in nine senior secondary schools in Benin City, Nigeria, June to July 2024. First year senior secondary students (about age 15) attended up to twelve 90 minute after school lab sessions over six weeks, working in pairs with Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) on English topics aligned to the national curriculum. Each session opened with a teacher provided prompt designed to make the model act as a tutor, not an answer giver, using learning science principles such as retrieval practice; teachers circulated and kept students on task, and sessions closed with group reflection. Teachers received three days of training. Result: 0.31 standard deviation gain on a combined assessment (0.23 on English), equal to roughly 1.5 to 2 years of typical schooling, placing it among the most cost effective education programs. Largest gains for girls and higher achieving students. Worked despite internet and power outages.

papers.why: Best evidence in the library that AI aimed at the adult, not the child, improves learning, and that it helps the least experienced adults most. Directly supports the book's Chapter 20 argument that AI should raise teacher and tutor quality, and gives a cost figure a board member can compare against a $3,300 per teacher PD program the authors cite.
papers.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
papers.venue: arXiv (cs.CL), Stanford
papers.caveat: Preprint, chat based tutoring platform, one district, two months, novice tutors. Proximal outcomes improved; end of year tests did not. Effects depend on tutors actually using the tool.
papers.finding: First randomized controlled trial of a human and AI system in live K12 tutoring: 900 novice tutors and 1,800 students from historically under served communities (majority Hispanic) in a Southern US school district, two months, math, preregistered. Tutor CoPilot gives the human tutor real time, expert like suggestions, not the student. Students of tutors with access were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics (62 to 66 percent exit ticket pass rate); students of lower rated tutors gained 9 points; students of tutors who actually used it gained 14 points. Cost was about $20 per tutor per year. Across 550,000 messages, tutors with access asked more guiding questions and gave away fewer answers. Tutors flagged suggestions that were not grade level appropriate or were too advanced. No significant effect on end of year state math scores.

papers.why: Important null result: short GenAI add-ons for self-regulation did not improve learning in secondary classrooms.
papers.title: Enhancing School Students' Self-Regulated Learning through Generative AI Support: A Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.venue: Educational Psychology Review
papers.finding: RCT with 371 German grade 7-9 students, six 45-minute sessions. GenAI supports targeting motivation or learning strategies did not beat plain ChatGPT on effort, knowledge, or strategy use; the utility-value version helped perceived value, and meaningful engagement linked to sustained interest.

papers.why: Concrete design for a guardrailed primary math tutor; supports testing in real classrooms, not just simulations.
papers.title: Taming the black box: Design principles for rule-integrated LLM tutoring systems in primary school mathematical problem solving
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Rule-guided LLM math tutor for primary word problems: diagnosis, then intent selection, then constrained response. Simulations and a pilot with 40 Grade 5 students showed more consistent scaffolding, fewer premature answers, and sustained engagement. Classroom pilot surfaced fragmented inputs and attention swings missed in simulation.

papers.why: Background on thinking outcomes.
papers.title: The cognitive impact of ChatGPT in higher education: A systematic review of critical and creative thinking outcomes
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Systematic review of ChatGPT effects on critical and creative thinking in higher education.

papers.why: School climate shapes later AI dependence; autonomy support matters in high school.
papers.title: How high-school pressure and autonomy support are linked to dual AI learning pathways: A cross-contextual SEM analysis
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: 508 university students recalling high school: high-school pressure linked to controlled motivation, then compulsive AI use and lower wellbeing; autonomy support linked to constructive use.

papers.why: Supports metacognition focus.
papers.title: Learning-to-learn in the age of generative AI: A scoping review and conceptual framework
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Scoping review and framework for learning-to-learn with GenAI.

papers.why: Background.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence agents in computer-supported collaborative learning: A systematic literature review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Systematic review of AI agents in computer-supported collaborative learning.

papers.why: Background on hallucination risk.
papers.title: A systematic review of the impact of GenAI on learning performance, AI hallucinations, and problem-solving in computer science education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Systematic review of GenAI in CS education: performance, hallucinations, problem solving.

papers.why: Performance is not learning. Students prefer the tool that helps them less.
papers.title: Less stress, better scores, same learning: The dissociation of performance and learning in AI-supported programming education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 10 (2026) 100537
papers.caveat: University CS1 course (N=275), single 90-minute exercise; two-item cognitive load subscales had limited reliability per authors.
papers.finding: RCT (N=275, university CS1). Both a hint-first tutor and ChatGPT raised exercise scores but neither raised learning; only the hint-first tutor raised intrinsic motivation. Students preferred ChatGPT.

papers.title: A systematic review of AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 education
papers.venue: npj Science of Learning
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: 28 quasi-experimental K-12 studies, 4,597 students: intelligent tutoring effects generally positive but smaller when compared with non-intelligent tutoring systems.

papers.why: Warning about offloading; supports hints-not-answers and metacognition.
papers.title: AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking
papers.venue: Societies
papers.finding: 666 participants: frequent AI use correlated with lower critical thinking, mediated by cognitive offloading; younger people more dependent.

papers.why: Dosage finding is useful if it holds.
papers.title: Enhancing Learning Outcomes through AI-Based Tutoring Systems: A Study on Student Motivation and Academic Achievement
papers.venue: ACADEMIA International Journal for Social Sciences
papers.caveat: Low-profile journal; results not independently verified. This is not verified.
papers.finding: Reported randomized trial (N=602, grades 7-10): adaptive tutoring raised achievement (d about 0.40), more for low-baseline students, gains leveled after about 12 hours.

papers.why: Learning-by-teaching is a strong alternative to answer-giving tutors.
papers.title:
Development of a generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    ‐powered teachable agent for middle school mathematics learning: A design‐based research study
papers.venue: British Journal of Educational Technology
papers.finding: Design-based research, 320 middle school students: a GenAI teachable agent (students teach the AI) produced larger knowledge gains than control in the final quasi-experiment.

papers.why: Human-supervised AI tutoring works: the tutor approves each message. Fits the human review gate.
papers.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
papers.venue: arXiv
papers.caveat: Preprint by a vendor research team; small sample.
papers.finding: Exploratory RCT, 165 students in five UK secondary schools on a math platform. Expert tutors supervised a pedagogy-tuned model and approved 76% of drafts with minimal edits. Students did at least as well as with human tutors and were 5.5 points more likely to solve novel problems.

papers.why: Strongest RCT showing a pedagogy-designed AI tutor can beat good human teaching, but only when designed with learning science.
papers.title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
papers.venue: Scientific Reports
papers.caveat: College students, one course, custom tutor.
papers.finding: Harvard physics RCT: college students using a custom AI tutor built on the same pedagogy as active-learning classes learned significantly more in less time and felt more engaged.

papers.why: Realistic effect size for K-12 math AI to set expectations.
papers.title: The Effectiveness of AI on K-12 Students’ Mathematics Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.venue: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of 21 K-12 math studies: small positive effect of AI (0.34), larger for intelligent tutoring and adaptive systems.

papers.why: Group work tools should prompt planning and self-checks, not just content.
papers.title: Examining the interplay of knowledge construction and group-level regulation in a computer-supported collaborative learning physics task
papers.venue: Computers in Human Behavior, vol 138
papers.finding: 34 secondary students in groups built a physics poster on an interactive tabletop. Group-level regulation (planning, task understanding, strategy, evaluation) guided and supported knowledge construction.

papers.why: Background.
papers.title: Temporally-focused analytics of self-regulated learning: A systematic review of literature
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Review of 53 studies on temporal analysis of self-regulated learning data.

papers.why: Background on national personalization trends.
papers.title: Personalized education and Artificial Intelligence in the United States, China, and India: A systematic review using a Human-In-The-Loop model
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Systematic review with human-in-the-loop NLP of 2019-2021 literature on AI personalization in the US, China, and India.

papers.why: Secondary evidence for personalized paths.
papers.title: The use of a personalized learning approach to implementing self-regulated online learning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Quasi-experiment in secondary physics: personalized learning paths within self-regulated online learning raised post-test and learning gains over conventional online learning.

papers.why: Supports light gamification for motivation.
papers.title: The effectiveness of gamification in programming education: Evidence from a meta-analysis
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of 21 studies: gamification in programming education has positive effects, largest on motivation, then achievement.

papers.why: Supports spaced, adaptive retrieval practice.
papers.title: Adaptive formative assessment system based on computerized adaptive testing and the learning memory cycle for personalized learning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Adaptive formative assessment combining computerized adaptive testing with memory-cycle review beat CAT alone and non-adaptive tests in a 7-week university programming course.

papers.why: Background for collaboration ideas.
papers.title: A systematic review of artificial intelligence techniques for collaborative learning over the past two decades
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Review of 41 studies on AI for collaborative learning: outcomes and social interaction uses, nine technique types.

papers.why: Supports adaptive hints that keep challenge right-sized.
papers.title: AI-Induced guidance: Preserving the optimal Zone of Proximal Development
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Discovery-learning game where AI adapted instruction text in real time kept learners in their zone of proximal development: higher learning, lower cognitive load, same enjoyment versus static instructions.

papers.why: Names a real risk of adaptive practice: it can make students passive. Supports a fade-the-scaffold design rule.
papers.title: The concept of hybrid human-AI regulation: Exemplifying how to support young learners’ self-regulated learning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.caveat: Concept and prototype, not yet evaluated.
papers.finding: Proposes Hybrid Human-AI Regulation (HHAIR) for learners aged 10-14 using adaptive learning tech. Most adaptive systems take over regulation from students; HHAIR gradually transfers regulation from AI to the learner so self-regulated learning skills grow.

papers.why: Background only.
papers.title: Directions of the 100 most cited chatbot-related human behavior research: A review of academic publications
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Review of top 100 cited chatbot papers and research trends.

papers.why: Pre-generative baseline for school chatbot uses such as FAQ, office front desk, and course questions.
papers.title: Chatbots applications in education: A systematic review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Review of 53 studies. Chatbots used for teaching and learning, admin, student support, and assessment. Benefits: quick personalized answers, integrated content, access. Challenges: ethics, evaluation, user attitudes, programming complexity, supervision and maintenance.

papers.why: Background for the adaptive practice theme; reinforces the prototype-to-practice gap.
papers.title: AI-enabled adaptive learning systems: A systematic mapping of the literature
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Mapping, not effect evaluation; mostly higher ed.
papers.finding: Mapping of 147 studies (2014-2020) on AI-enabled adaptive learning. Identifies intervention types and common analytic techniques, and notes few systems are actually implemented to address real student problems.

children.name: Supervised Tutoring in Class
children.blurb: Supervised tutoring in class means students work with a school configured AI tutor while a teacher is present in the room and moving among them.

children.name: Homework Help With Visible Logs
children.blurb: Homework help with visible logs means a homework tool configured by the school gives hints rather than answers and records each conversation for teacher review.

children.name: Learning Paths With Teacher Override
children.blurb: Learning paths with teacher override means adaptive software adjusts what each student works on next based on how they are doing, but the teacher can step in and change that path.

children.name: Handing Regulation Back to Students
children.blurb: Handing regulation back to students means that adaptive software and the teacher gradually give the student control over learning decisions instead of letting the system make them all.

children.name: Study Tools and Planning
children.blurb: Study tools and planning means using AI to turn a student's own notes and a teacher's materials into flashcards, practice questions, and quizzes, and to help students break projects into steps and reflect after tests.

children.name: Knowing What Students Know
children.blurb: Knowing what students know means giving teachers a fast, current picture of where each student stands before they plan the next lesson.

children.name: Formats, Examples, and Avatars
children.blurb: This idea covers three ways to make personalized lessons more accessible and meaningful: offering content in multiple formats, using AI to suggest examples connected to students' lives, and choosing tutor avatars carefully.

children.name: Enrichment, Peer Tutoring, and Group Work
children.blurb: This idea covers three ways AI can support students beyond remediation: enrichment for advanced learners, peer tutoring, and group projects.

children.name: Students in Special Situations
children.blurb: This idea covers students who need support outside the usual school flow: those who miss several days, high school students making up failed courses, and students who are homebound or in the hospital.

children.name: Equity: Devices, Internet, and Time
children.blurb: Equity in personalized learning means making sure every student can actually use the tools, not just handing the same tool to everyone.

children.name: Testing a Tutor Before Students Use It
children.blurb: Testing a tutor before students use it means a teacher tries to break the setup by acting like a struggling student, asking for answers and making mistakes.

children.name: Measuring Whether Personalization Works
children.blurb: Measuring whether personalization works means judging a tutoring or personalized learning tool by what students can do on their own, not by how often they log in.

children.name: What Families Should Know
children.blurb: Families should know which tutoring tools their children use and how those tools are set up, including that the tools give hints rather than answers, that teachers can see conversation logs, and how student information is protected.

children.name: Personalization Without Burning Out Teachers
children.blurb: Personalization can add hidden work for teachers through looking at logs, changing learning paths, checking generated materials, and planning small groups.

sections.body: This section is about one to one tutoring, the long standing hope that technology could give every student the kind of help only the wealthy could once buy, and what AI is actually doing in that space. The book describes AI tutoring as a tool that can extend what teachers do for each student, not a machine handed to each child in place of a teacher. It covers supervised tutoring in class, homework help, adaptive learning paths, self regulation and planning, study tools, support for students in special situations, and the equity questions that come with any tool used at home. The clearest success came from after school sessions in Nigeria, where students worked in pairs with an AI chat tool, teachers wrote the opening prompt so the tool acted as a tutor, and teachers circulated the whole time. A United Kingdom trial found an AI tutor supervised by expert human tutors did at least as well as human tutoring alone, though the company that built the model ran that study.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that the successes shared one feature: adults designed how the tool was used and stayed involved. When students used a plain chatbot on their own, the results were very different, as the high school math trial showed, where the unguarded group scored worse on a later exam without AI. The common failure pattern is the unsupervised tutor, where a district buys a tool, gives every student access at home, and counts logins as success while the students who need the most help either cannot reach it or use it to get answers. The rule the book holds to is that personalized learning is not about handing each student a machine, it is about using machines to extend what teachers can do for each student. Two ideas carry strong evidence, several more have promising early support, and the rest are practices to pilot carefully.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from the classroom outward to the home and the district. Supervised Tutoring in Class and Homework Help With Visible Logs cover the two settings where the evidence is strongest, and Learning Paths With Teacher Override and Handing Regulation Back to Students show how much control a teacher keeps over what the tool decides. Study Tools and Planning, Knowing What Students Know, Formats, Examples, and Avatars, and Enrichment, Peer Tutoring, and Group Work cover the study and design questions a teacher would bring to a tool before using it. Students in Special Situations and Equity: Devices, Internet, and Time are for the leader asking who actually benefits, and Testing a Tutor Before Students Use It and Measuring Whether Personalization Works give the leader the checks to run before and after adoption. What Families Should Know and Personalization Without Burning Out Teachers are for the parent and the teacher who have to live with the tool every day.
sections.heading: How these pages fit together
